item.title: Stochastic coupling of climate variables and ice volume over the Late Pleistocene glacial cycles
item.dc:creator: Pijush Patra, L. T. Giorgini, J. S. Wettlaufer
item.category: Chaos An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science
item.description:
Chaos An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science — matched: ice sheet, ice dynamics, cryosphere, paleoclimate, interglacial, glacial cycle, oxygen isotope, climate feedback
Understanding the interactions between ice sheets and global climate forcings over geological timescales is essential for projecting their future. Previous studies have highlighted the role of ice dynamics and climate interactions in establishing the 100 000-year glacial cycles, particularly regarding the growth of North American ice sheets. Researchers have reconstructed consistent time series for ice volume, temperature, and carbon dioxide by applying inverse forward modeling to benthic oxygen isotope records. In this paper, we model the stochastic behavior of paleoclimate time series to evaluate the coupling between climate variables during the Pleistocene glacial cycles. We quantify the behavior of these time series using multifractal time-weighted detrended fluctuation analysis, which differentiates between near-red-noise and white-noise behavior below and above the 100 000-year glacial cycle, respectively, in all records. This study builds upon the work of Keyes et al. [Chaos 33, 093132 (2023)] by incorporating ice volume into a five-variable model that includes carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, and temperature, along with intervariable coupling terms to capture potential relationships among these variables. To test our model, we compute response functions for each pair of variables and compare them with empirical data, confirming our predictions regarding intervariable stability and coupling. This study provides a comprehensive overview of glacial-interglacial dynamics and highlights the role of cryosphere-climate feedbacks in shaping Earth's climate evolution.

item.title: A large ice‐dammed lake in the western Danish North Sea: Deglacial evolution and ice‐margin dynamics
item.dc:creator: Lasse Tésik Prins, Lis Allaart, Katrine Elnegaard Hansen, Katrine Juul Andresen, Ole Bennike, Bodil W. Lauridsen, … (+1)
item.description:
Journal of Quaternary Science — matched: ice sheet, ice flow, deglaciation, last glacial maximum, LGM, Holocene, Quaternary
Abstract The Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) ice extent in the western Danish North Sea remains unchartered, which impedes our understanding of the last glacial to Holocene transition in the region. Despite increasing interest in the shallow subsurface of the North Sea, there is still a knowledge gap concerning this transition. In this study, we describe the geological evolution of the southern part of the western Danish North Sea using high‐resolution seismic data, with emphasis on the LGM and the late Quaternary development. We have identified a large glaciotectonic complex that delineates the maximum extent of the LGM ice sheet and indicates a general NNW‐SSE ice flow direction. We describe the drainage history associated with a large ice‐dammed lake, which covered most of the southern North Sea, presumably lasting for more than 2000 years from the LGM until ~19 cal kyrs BP. Based on the interpreted seismic profiles and regional depositional and deformational patterns, we provide a model for how the deglaciation unfolded in the western Danish North Sea. The deglacial sequence of events is placed into a late Quaternary context and related to the existing stratigraphic models for the area. Our study sheds new light on the distribution of potentially challenging buried landscapes for offshore construction and windfarm development.

item.title: Extreme cold–dry events in East Asia during glacials reflect insolation thresholds
item.dc:creator: Hao Lu, Jingjing Guo, Qiuzhen Yin, Louise Fuchs, Zhipeng Wu, Youbin Sun, … (+2)
item.description:
Communications Earth & Environment — matched: critical threshold, orbital forcing, insolation, proxy, climate extreme
Abstract Whether extreme climate events reflect intrinsic threshold behaviour of the climate system remains uncertain, in part because most terrestrial archives integrate multiple climatic signals and lack simultaneous constraints on temperature and hydroclimate. Here we present high-resolution ( ~ 900 years) quantitative reconstructions of land temperature and monsoon precipitation from the Chinese Loess Plateau spanning the past ~250,000 years, based on molecular fossil proxies. Using branched glycerol dialkyl glycerol tetraether (brGDGT) proxies for temperature and precipitation, together with complementary GDGT-based aridity indicators, our records reveal repeated extreme cold–dry events during glacial inceptions, in addition to pronounced droughts during glacial terminations. Although previous studies have provided key insights into past monsoon variability, these cold–dry extremes are not clearly expressed in widely used terrestrial proxies such as speleothem δ¹⁸O records, indicating that key aspects of continental climate variability have remained under-recognized. Transient climate simulations reproduce the timing of the extreme cooling events, providing model-based support for threshold-like climate responses to declining boreal summer insolation. Our findings suggest that such threshold-like behaviour may represent an important mode of continental climate responses to orbital forcing, providing a long-term perspective for assessing how regional climate extremes may emerge when background conditions approach critical thresholds.

item.title: Improved subglacial boundary conditions near Dome C, Antarctica, through rigorous integration of multi-campaign radar data and an ensemble stochastic simulation approach
item.dc:creator: Calvin Shackleton, Kenichi Matsuoka, Brett Fraysher, Joohan Lee, Jørgen Dall, Allain Rapadas, … (+5)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: ice sheet, subglacial, Antarctic, Antarctica, ensemble
We map new details of the landscape beneath the Antarctic Ice Sheet near Dome C using radar data and simulation methods. The terrain is rougher than previously thought, and we identify where water flow is either well or poorly understood. We also show that valleys and ridges could amplify or reduce geothermal heating, impacting melting at the ice sheet base. These results improve confidence in locating sites where ancient ice may be preserved for drilling and studying past climates.

item.title: The implementation and effectiveness of Calving Algorithms in numerical ice models (CalvingMIP)
item.dc:creator: James R. Jordan, Frank Pattyn, Daniel Abele, Torsten Albrecht, Jorge Alvarez-Solas, Jowan M. Barnes, … (+24)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: ice sheet, calving, sea level, sea-level rise
Ice calving is a recent inclusion in ice sheet models and there has not been a systematic test of how well it has been implemented. We show that models can accurately represent a given rate of ice calving, properties at the ice front evolve smoothly during calving, and that there are no consistent differences in ice behaviour between various approaches to representing calving in numerical ice models. This gives us confidence in their ability for use in sea level rise prediction simulations.

item.title: Tree-ring cellulose oxygen isotope reveals summer hydroclimate variability across the East European Plain
item.dc:creator: Qiaoyun Lin, Chenxi Xu, Ru Huang, Wenling An, Vladimir Matskovsky, Olga Solomina, … (+3)
item.description:
Climate of the Past — matched: oxygen isotope
Along the East European Plain latitudinal transect, Scots pine tree-ring cellulose oxygen isotopes (δ18OTRC) increases from north to south and consistently records significant summer hydroclimate signals. Although the dominant controls differ among regions, the northern chronology shows the strongest and most stable vapor pressure deficit signal. Compared with tree-ring width (TRW), δ18OTRC better reflects regional climate information linked to atmospheric humidity and evaporative demand.

item.title: Quaternary Palm Fossils from Coastal Florida, USA: A 2016 Hurricane as a Tool for Paleontology Research
item.dc:creator: George Mustoe, Leslie Maxwell, Geri Maxwell
item.description:
Geosciences — matched: Holocene, Quaternary, radiocarbon
In October 2016, Hurricane Matthew passed along the east coast of Florida, USA. Intense coastal erosion by storm waves made sandy beaches to reveal a multitude of trunk molds of ancient palm trees that once flourished along what is now the intertidal zone. A combination of coastal engineering efforts and natural processes caused the ancient palms to be reburied by beach sand. Fortunately, two retired geologists quickly responded after the hurricane ended, conducting a detailed investigation of the fossil palms. The trunk molds occur in two adjacent parallel zones that have an overall length of 1.4 km. The seaward-facing zone contains trunk molds where wood has been mineralized by calcite, enclosed within a coquinoid outer zone. The molds are associated with areas of gray coquina. In contrast, the landward-facing zone is characterized by trunk molds that contain mummified wood tissues within a weakly cemented sand matrix. These molds have thin coquina outer boundaries, but they occur within loose beach sand. Geological and botanical characteristics suggest a Holocene age for the ancient palm groves; their occurrence and demise are associated with small-scale regression/transgression cycles. A 14C radiocarbon age of 160 yrs BP for one of the younger cycles suggests the possibility that the landward- facing coastal palm growth was related to tidal changes that were related to the temperature fluctuations of the Little Ice Age (1300–1850).

item.title: Effects of snow redistribution parameterization on simulated snow thickness validated by MOSAiC observations
item.dc:creator: Fengguan Gu, Changwei Liu, Bo Han, Qinghua Yang, Jiping Liu
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: Arctic, sea ice, parameterization
Snow on Arctic sea ice acts like a blanket that traps heat and reflects sunlight, so it matters for the climate. Drawing on measurements from a year-long Arctic expedition, we improved models that simulate snow on the ice. Without wind-driven snow movement, the models overestimated snow depth. Adding a wind-driven scheme cut the average error by more than half. After tuning, simulated snow matched observations. The findings help project how Arctic sea ice may evolve in a warming climate.

item.title: Cacti are severely threatened by drought in a warming world
item.description:
Nature — matched: extreme event, climate change
Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03496-z Forecasts of the effects that climate change will have on biodiversity typically rely on long-term climate averages while excluding extreme events. Projections that include severe drought predict that a majority of the 993 cactus species assessed will see large losses of suitable climatic area: more than 25% of species could lose at least 80% of it by 2100.

item.title: Multi-sensor satellite analysis reveals latitudinal and morphometric controls on ice phenology across 31 000 lakes on the Alaska North Slope
item.dc:creator: Alexander L. Nguyen, Cesar G. Lopez, Jennifer Melara-Valle, Eliza Ross, Alexander S. Bradley, Maggie R. Limbeck, … (+2)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: Arctic, greenhouse gas, machine learning
Arctic lakes undergo freezing and thawing, but the timing and duration of these events across large areas is not well known. Using a machine learning model applied to satellite imagery, we successfully identify lake ice conditions on over 30 000 lakes in Alaska with high accuracy. Our results indicate that latitude is an important control on lake ice conditions, with secondary effects from lake size and shape. These findings have implications for future greenhouse gas emissions in the Arctic.

item.title: Temporal Dynamics of Sediment Characteristics in the Proglacial River of Gangotri Glacier: Impacts of Ablation and Climate Variability
item.dc:creator: Jatin Malhotra, Manohar Arora, Narendra Kumar Goel
item.description:
Hydrological Sciences Journal — matched: glacier
Surface debris exerts profound influence on glacial dynamics as it changes the surface ablation and spatial distribution rates. This paper addresses the temporal variation in particle size distribution, sediment load (SSL), suspended sediment concentration (SSC) in the heading stream that flows out of the Glacier for the period (2017, 2018, 2019, 2022, 2023). Analysis of the data shows an increasing trend of SSC in relation to discharge since June and highest sediment load occurring in July and August. Silt particles (31–80%) followed by sand (18–45%) and clay (1–4%) dominated the suspended sediments. The proportions of sand particles were found to be less variable, whereas the proportion of the clay particles varied greatly when historical data of two distinct melt seasons (2004–2006 & 2017–2019) were compared. The poorly sorted sediments delivered are indicative of intense glacial erosion and kurtosis values during the melt seasoning suggest the climatic variations influence the area.

item.title: Quantifying charger-related uncertainty in electrical mobility analysis of aerosols with MPSS-UQ 1.0
item.dc:creator: Matti Niskanen, Aku Ursin, Arttu Ylisirniö, Kari Erkki Juhani Lehtinen
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: Bayesian
Measuring tiny airborne particles by their movement in an electric field is common in atmospheric science, but the results almost never include uncertainty estimates. The largest source of uncertainty in these measurements relates to particle charging. We developed a Bayesian method to systematically quantify this uncertainty. Applied to a month of atmospheric data, accounting for charging uncertainty widened the plausible range of particle concentrations by a factor of two to ten.
